# Salpingitis Isthmica Nodosa

**Authors:** David Barkwill, Kyle J. Tobler

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Salpingitis isthmica nodosa, occasionally referred to as diverticulosis of the fallopian tube, has an incidence of 0.6% to 11% in healthy, fertile women and is strongly associated with both infertility and ectopic pregnancies. The etiology of salpingitis isthmica nodosa is still debated; however, the cause is likely due to an acquired process. The management of salpingitis isthmica nodosa is aimed at restoring and maintaining fertility. Anatomy Fallopian tubes typically range from 10 to 14 cm in length and have an external diameter of approximately 1 cm. They are described as having 4 different parts: the fimbriae, infundibulum, ampulla, and isthmus, which connect the fallopian tubes to the uterus. The lumen at the isthmus is relatively small (1-2 mm) and is surrounded by a 3-layered muscular wall. This consists of a middle circular layer sandwiched between inner and outer longitudinal layers. Salpingitis isthmica nodosa causes nodular swelling (up to a few centimeters in diameter) predominantly at the isthmus; however, it can involve all other portions of the fallopian tube. The outer serosa of the nodules are smooth and yellow, grey, or brown in color.
